content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, the wall most commonly symbolizes protection, security, and salvation—especially the defense God himself provides for his people. Ancient city walls were the primary guarantee of a city's safety, so the wall becomes an image of divine safeguarding: God is a 'wall of fire' around Jerusalem, salvation itself is called walls and bulwarks, and the walled New Jerusalem pictures the perfect security and inviolability of God's redeemed people. Conversely, a broken or missing wall symbolizes vulnerability, judgment, and defenselessness.", "primary_basis": ["Isaiah 26:1 ('salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks')", "Isaiah 60:18 ('you shall call your walls Salvation, and your gates Praise')", "Zechariah 2:4-5 (the LORD as 'a wall of fire' around Jerusalem)", "Psalm 51:18 (prayer to 'build up the walls of Jerusalem')", "Revelation 21:12-18 (the great high wall of the New Jerusalem)", "Proverbs 25:28 (a person without self-control is 'like a city broken into and left without walls')", "Nehemiah 1-6 (rebuilding Jerusalem's wall as restoration and renewed security under God)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Separation and division: the wall as a barrier of hostility between groups (Jew and Gentile) or between humanity and God, which Christ demolishes. This is the standard New Testament theological use in Ephesians and is heavily preached, often described as 'the dividing wall' broken down by the cross.", "basis": ["Ephesians 2:14 ('has broken down the dividing wall of hostility')", "Often linked homiletically to the temple's soreg (barrier excluding Gentiles)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Obstacle or barrier to faith and obedience that God overcomes or enables believers to overcome, drawn chiefly from the fall of Jericho's walls; frequently used in sermons about faith conquering impossible circumstances ('walls come tumbling down').", "basis": ["Joshua 6:1-20 (the walls of Jericho fall)", "Hebrews 11:30 ('by faith the walls of Jericho fell down')", "Psalm 18:29 / 2 Samuel 22:30 ('by my God I can leap over a wall')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Broken walls as an image of divine judgment, sin's consequences, and personal vulnerability or lack of self-control; rebuilding walls as repentance, restoration, and re-establishing spiritual boundaries (a staple of preaching on Nehemiah).", "basis": ["Proverbs 25:28", "Lamentations 2:8-9 (the LORD determined to destroy the wall)", "Nehemiah 1:3; 2:17", "Isaiah 5:5 (God removes the vineyard's wall in judgment)", "Ezekiel 13:10-15 (whitewashed wall of false prophets)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "False security or hypocrisy: the 'whitewashed wall'—an outwardly plastered but structurally unsound wall—as an image of false prophets and hypocrites, echoed in Paul's rebuke of the high priest.", "basis": ["Ezekiel 13:10-16", "Acts 23:3 ('God will strike you, you whitewashed wall')", "cf. Matthew 23:27 (whitewashed tombs, often linked)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "The Church or the individual believer as a wall—strength, maturity, and chastity—drawn from the Song of Songs ('I am a wall') and from intercessors who 'stand in the gap' in the wall, an image of prophetic or priestly mediation.", "basis": ["Song of Songs 8:9-10", "Ezekiel 22:30 ('stand in the gap' / 'build up the wall')", "Jeremiah 1:18; 15:20 (the prophet made 'a fortified bronze wall')"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "medium", "notes": "The wall is a polyvalent biblical image whose meaning is strongly context-dependent, so no single reading is exclusive. Nevertheless, the protection/security/salvation sense is the most widely recognized default in commentaries, Bible dictionaries (e.g., Dictionary of Biblical Imagery entries), and preaching, grounded in the realities of ancient walled cities. The Ephesians 2 'dividing wall' and the Jericho 'obstacle' readings are also very widely used but are typically treated as passage-specific applications rather than the general symbolic meaning. Confidence is medium rather than high because the term's polyvalence means different traditions foreground different senses (e.g., ecumenical and reconciliation contexts foreground Ephesians 2)."}
